notation.meaning: Log of the series (e.g. real GDP)
Cyclical component, percent deviation from trend

notationIntro: *US real GDP with its HP trend (left) and the log deviations from trend (right).*

blocks.md: GDP grows over decades and wiggles around that growth from year to year. To study recessions and booms, economists separate the two: a smooth trend line through the data, and the deviations from it, the "cycle". The Hodrick-Prescott filter draws the trend by balancing two goals: stay close to the data, but don't bend too sharply. A single number decides the balance; the larger it is, the straighter the trend and the more movement is counted as cycle. Business-cycle models are typically judged on these deviations only, which means they are not asked to explain the trend at all.

blocks.title: Why it matters
blocks.md: Most stylized facts about business cycles, and the apparent fit of the RBC model, are statements about HP-filtered data.
The lecture describes the filter as "a kind of moving average". (Beyond the lecture:) for a (log) series $y_t = \tau_t + c_t$, the trend $\tau_t$ solves
and the cycle is $c_t = y_t - \tau_t$. With $\lambda = 0$ the trend is the data; as $\lambda \to \infty$ it becomes a straight line. Conventional values: 1,600 (quarterly), 100 or 6.25 (annual).

- **Treating the cycle as a fact of nature.** It depends on $\lambda$ and on the filter; it can create spurious cycles and behaves badly at the ends of the sample.
- **Asking a model to fit filtered data and calling that a full test.** The trend, and the transition between trend and cycle, are left unexplained.
